claim: Mitochondrial complex I has a key role in cellular energy metabolism, generating a major portion of the proton motive force that drives aerobic ATP synthesis.
source: Mitochondrial complex I has a key role in cellular energy metabolism, generating a major portion of the proton motive force that drives aerobic ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about complex I function.

claim: The hydrophilic arm of complex I transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone.
source: The hydrophilic arm of the L-shaped ~1 MDa membrane protein complex transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone, providing the energy to drive proton pumping at distant sites in the membrane arm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the electron transfer function of complex I.

claim: Electron transfer from NADH to ubiquinone provides the energy to drive proton pumping at distant sites in the membrane arm.
source: The hydrophilic arm of the L-shaped ~1 MDa membrane protein complex transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone, providing the energy to drive proton pumping at distant sites in the membrane arm.
evidence: This describes the coupling mechanism between electron transfer and proton pumping based on established knowledge.

claim: The critical steps of energy conversion in complex I are associated with the redox chemistry of ubiquinone.
source: The critical steps of energy conversion are associated with the redox chemistry of ubiquinone.
evidence: This is a statement based on established understanding of complex I mechanism.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of complete mitochondrial complex I from Y. lipolytica was obtained in the deactive form.
source: We report the cryo-EM structure of complete mitochondrial complex I from the aerobic yeast Yarrowia lipolytica both in the deactive form and after capturing the enzyme during steady-state activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A cryo-EM structure of complete mitochondrial complex I from Y. lipolytica was obtained during steady-state activity.
source: We report the cryo-EM structure of complete mitochondrial complex I from the aerobic yeast Yarrowia lipolytica both in the deactive form and after capturing the enzyme during steady-state activity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The site of ubiquinone binding observed during turnover supports a two-state stabilization change mechanism for complex I.
source: The site of ubiquinone binding observed during turnover supports a two-state stabilization change mechanism for complex I.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data presented in the study.

claim: Respiratory complex I is a ~1 MDa membrane protein complex.
source: Respiratory complex I is a ~1 MDa membrane protein complex with key functions in aerobic energy metabolism (Hirst, 2013; Wirth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: Fourteen central subunits of complex I are conserved from bacteria to mammals.
source: Fourteen central subunits are conserved from bacteria to mammals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I structure.

claim: Mitochondrial complex I contains around 30 accessory subunits in addition to the 14 central subunits.
source: Mitochondrial complex I contains in addition around 30 accessory subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial complex I composition.

claim: The energy released in the electron transfer reaction from NADH to ubiquinone is utilized to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane or the bacterial cell membrane.
source: The energy released in the electron transfer reaction from NADH to ubiquinone is utilized to pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane or the bacterial cell membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I function.

claim: The electrochemical gradient established by redox-coupled proton translocation drives ATP synthesis.
source: The electrochemical gradient established by redox-coupled proton translocation drives ATP synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bioenergetics.

claim: Dysfunction of complex I is implicated in a number of neuromuscular and degenerative diseases.
source: Dysfunction of complex I is implicated in a number of neuromuscular and degenerative diseases (Rodenburg, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In myocardial infarction, complex I releases detrimental reactive oxygen species (ROS) that contribute to reperfusion injury.
source: In myocardial infarction, complex I releases detrimental reactive oxygen species (ROS) that contribute to reperfusion injury (Chouchani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The reversible conversion of the active A-form of complex I into the deactive D-form (A/D transition) is thought to minimize ROS formation.
source: The reversible conversion of the active A-form of complex I into the deactive D-form (A/D transition) (Kotlyar and Vinogradov, 1990) is thought to minimize ROS formation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous literature.

claim: X-ray structures of bacterial complex I were solved at 3.3 Å resolution.
source: X-ray structures of bacterial complex I (Baradaran et al., 2013) and of the mitochondrial complex I from the aerobic yeast Yarrowia lipolytica (Zickermann et al., 2015) were solved at 3.3 and 3.6 to 3.9 Å resolution, respectively.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: X-ray structures of mitochondrial complex I from Y. lipolytica were solved at 3.6 to 3.9 Å resolution.
source: X-ray structures of bacterial complex I (Baradaran et al., 2013) and of the mitochondrial complex I from the aerobic yeast Yarrowia lipolytica (Zickermann et al., 2015) were solved at 3.3 and 3.6 to 3.9 Å resolution, respectively.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Recent technical progress has permitted the structure of mammalian complex I to be determined at 3.3 to 4.2 Å resolution by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: Recent technical progress has permitted the structure of mammalian complex I by itself or as part of a supercomplex to be determined at 3.3 to 4.2 Å resolution by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) (Zhu et al., 2016; Fiedorczuk et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Letts et al., 2016; Guo et al., 2017; Blaza et al., 2018; Agip et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Essential mechanistic details of the catalytic cycle of complex I remain elusive.
source: Even though the structure of complex I is now well-characterized, essential mechanistic details of the catalytic cycle remain elusive, and conflicting models for the A/D transition have recently been proposed (Zickermann et al., 2015; Blaza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Conflicting models for the A/D transition have recently been proposed.
source: Even though the structure of complex I is now well-characterized, essential mechanistic details of the catalytic cycle remain elusive, and conflicting models for the A/D transition have recently been proposed (Zickermann et al., 2015; Blaza et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: There is general agreement that the reduction of ubiquinone at a position above the membrane bilayer triggers and drives proton translocation.
source: There is general agreement that the reduction of ubiquinone at a position above the membrane bilayer triggers and drives proton translocation, but it is not clear how this works.
evidence: This is a statement about the current consensus in the field.

claim: The mechanism by which ubiquinone reduction drives proton translocation is not clear.
source: There is general agreement that the reduction of ubiquinone at a position above the membrane bilayer triggers and drives proton translocation, but it is not clear how this works.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: The power stroke generated during ubiquinone reduction results from a concerted rearrangement of its binding site and the surrounding protein region, driven by the stabilization of anionic ubiquinone intermediates.
source: We hypothesized that the power stroke generated during ubiquinone reduction results from a concerted rearrangement of its binding site and the surrounding protein region, driven by the stabilization of anionic ubiquinone intermediates (Zickermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors and cited from their previous work.

claim: The proposed mechanism implies a cycling between two alternating ubiquinone binding sites during turnover.
source: This mechanism implies a cycling between two alternating ubiquinone binding sites during turnover, one of which (the E-state) selectively allows reduction and the other (the P-state), protonation of the ubiquinone headgroup.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: The E-state selectively allows reduction of the ubiquinone headgroup.
source: This mechanism implies a cycling between two alternating ubiquinone binding sites during turnover, one of which (the E-state) selectively allows reduction and the other (the P-state), protonation of the ubiquinone headgroup.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: The P-state selectively allows protonation of the ubiquinone headgroup.
source: This mechanism implies a cycling between two alternating ubiquinone binding sites during turnover, one of which (the E-state) selectively allows reduction and the other (the P-state), protonation of the ubiquinone headgroup.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model.

claim: The associated conformational changes are thought to polarize key residues at the start of a chain of conserved acidic and basic residues extending into and along the membrane arm.
source: The associated conformational changes are thought to polarize key residues at the start of a chain of conserved acidic and basic residues extending into and along the membrane arm, thus creating an electrostatic pulse (Euro et al., 2008) driving the proton pumping modules of complex I.
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous literature.

claim: Conformational changes create an electrostatic pulse driving the proton pumping modules of complex I.
source: The associated conformational changes are thought to polarize key residues at the start of a chain of conserved acidic and basic residues extending into and along the membrane arm, thus creating an electrostatic pulse (Euro et al., 2008) driving the proton pumping modules of complex I.
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from previous literature.

claim: A cryo-EM map of complex I purified from Y. lipolytica was obtained from 124,626 particle images and refined to 4.3 Å overall resolution.
source: A cryo-EM map of complex I purified from Y. lipolytica was obtained from 124,626 particle images and refined to 4.3 Å overall resolution (Figures 1–3, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results.

claim: Central parts of the complex I molecule were significantly better resolved than the overall resolution.
source: Central parts of the molecule were significantly better resolved (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing local resolution.

claim: The final model of complex I contains 42 subunits.
source: The final model of 42 subunits was 88% complete and contained 7515 fitted residues (Figure 4, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model composition.

claim: The final model of complex I was 88% complete and contained 7515 fitted residues.
source: The final model of 42 subunits was 88% complete and contained 7515 fitted residues (Figure 4, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model completeness.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of complex I agrees well with the previously determined X-ray structure in the deactive state (r.m.s.d. of 1.768 Å for central subunits).
source: The cryo-EM structure of complex I agrees well (r.m.s.d. of 1.768 Å for central subunits) with the previously determined X-ray structure in the deactive state, which was however much less complete with only 4979 residues fitted (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current structure with previous work.

claim: The X-ray structure of deactive complex I was much less complete with only 4979 residues fitted.
source: The cryo-EM structure of complex I agrees well (r.m.s.d. of 1.768 Å for central subunits) with the previously determined X-ray structure in the deactive state, which was however much less complete with only 4979 residues fitted (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work.

claim: Cryo-EM of mammalian complex I resolved several different conformations.
source: Whereas cryo-EM of mammalian complex I resolved several different conformations (Zhu et al., 2016; Fiedorczuk et al., 2016), we observed only one major class, indicating that the preparation of Y. lipolytica complex I was homogeneous and in a uniform state (Figure 1).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Only one major class was observed in the Y. lipolytica complex I preparation, indicating that the preparation was homogeneous and in a uniform state.
source: Whereas cryo-EM of mammalian complex I resolved several different conformations (Zhu et al., 2016; Fiedorczuk et al., 2016), we observed only one major class, indicating that the preparation of Y. lipolytica complex I was homogeneous and in a uniform state (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: About 30% of the particles belong to a subclass which contains the accessory sulfur transferase subunit ST1.
source: About 30% of the particles belong to a subclass (yellow) which contains the accessory sulfur transferase subunit ST1 known to be bound substoichiometrically to Y. lipolytica complex I (D'Imprima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: ST1 is known to be bound substoichiometrically to Y. lipolytica complex I.
source: About 30% of the particles belong to a subclass (yellow) which contains the accessory sulfur transferase subunit ST1 known to be bound substoichiometrically to Y. lipolytica complex I (D'Imprima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The overall structure of the fourteen central subunits is conserved in all known complex I structures.
source: The overall structure of the fourteen central subunits (Figure 4) is conserved in all known complex I structures.
evidence: This is a statement based on comparison with known structures.

claim: In mammalian and Y. lipolytica complex I the 49 kDa subunit harbors a long N-terminal extension that runs on the matrix side to approximately the middle of the membrane arm.
source: In mammalian and Y. lipolytica complex I the 49 kDa subunit harbors a long N-terminal extension that runs on the matrix side to approximately the middle of the membrane arm.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the current study.

claim: In Y. lipolytica, an N-terminal extension of the 30 kDa subunit reaches towards the attachment site of the accessory sulfur transferase subunit ST1.
source: In Y. lipolytica, an N-terminal extension of the 30 kDa subunit reaches towards the attachment site of the accessory sulfur transferase subunit ST1 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: A C-terminal sequence stretch of membrane-bound subunit ND3 extends vertically along the matrix arm, forming an elongated contact site with accessory subunit NUFM.
source: A C-terminal sequence stretch of membrane-bound subunit ND3 extends vertically along the matrix arm, forming an elongated contact site with accessory subunit NUFM (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The assignment of TMH4 of subunit ND6 was changed compared with the X-ray structure of Y. lipolytica complex I.
source: Compared with the X-ray structure of Y. lipolytica complex I (Zickermann et al., 2015) we changed the assignment of TMH4 of subunit ND6.
evidence: This is a statement about a change in the model compared to previous work.

claim: The corresponding helices match the X-ray structure of Thermus thermophilus and the cryo-EM structure of Y. lipolytica complex I but are shifted towards the peripheral arm in mammalian complex I.
source: The corresponding helices match the X-ray structure of Thermus thermophilus and the cryo-EM structure of Y. lipolytica complex I but are shifted towards the peripheral arm in mammalian complex I (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a comparison of structures shown in Figure 7.

claim: The absence of TMH1-3 of ND2 in mammalian complex I causes a conspicuous ambilateral indentation of the membrane arm that is not present in bacterial and yeast complex I.
source: In conjunction with the absence of TMH1-3 of ND2, this causes a conspicuous ambilateral indentation of the membrane arm of mammalian complex I that is not present in bacterial and yeast complex I.
evidence: This is a structural comparison between different species.

claim: Density for all expected 28 accessory subunits of Y. lipolytica complex I was identified.
source: We identified density for all expected 28 accessory subunits of Y. lipolytica complex I (Figure 8, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the structural findings.

claim: A new accessory subunit with a single transmembrane helix was detected in the membrane arm.
source: In the membrane arm we detected density for a new accessory subunit with a single transmembrane helix (provisionally labelled X in Figure 8).
evidence: This is a new structural finding reported in the study.

claim: All accessory subunits of Y. lipolytica complex I except subunits X, ST1 and NUXM were assigned to corresponding subunits of mammalian complex I based on sequence alignments and structural correlation.
source: With the exception of this previously unknown subunit and subunits ST1 and NUXM, all accessory subunits of Y. lipolytica complex I were assigned to corresponding subunits of mammalian complex I based on sequence alignments and structural correlation (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statement about the assignment process.

claim: For eighteen accessory subunits the cryo-EM map showed most or almost all (59–98%) of the side chain densities.
source: For eighteen accessory subunits the cryo-EM map showed most or almost all (59–98%) of the side chain densities (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the density map.

claim: Subunits NESM and NUZM have prominent extra domains.
source: Subunits NESM and NUZM have prominent extra domains and the NUFM subunit carries an N-terminal extension that interacts tightly with the C-terminal extension of central subunit ND3 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The NUFM subunit carries an N-terminal extension that interacts tightly with the C-terminal extension of central subunit ND3.
source: Subunits NESM and NUZM have prominent extra domains and the NUFM subunit carries an N-terminal extension that interacts tightly with the C-terminal extension of central subunit ND3 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: NI2M, NB5M and NIDM of Y. lipolytica are significantly smaller than their mammalian counterparts.
source: In contrast, NI2M, NB5M and NIDM of Y. lipolytica are significantly smaller.
evidence: This is a comparison with mammalian complex I.

claim: No density was found at positions of the mammalian 42 kDa subunit (NDUFA10), the 9 kDa subunit (NDUFV3), or the MNLL (NDUFB1) subunit.
source: We did not find any density at positions of the mammalian 42 kDa subunit (NDUFA10), the 9 kDa subunit (NDUFV3), or the MNLL (NDUFB1) subunit, consistent with the absence of their orthologs in the Y. lipolytica genome.
evidence: This is a structural observation consistent with genomic data.

claim: The absence of density for NDUFA10, NDUFV3, and NDUFB1 is consistent with the absence of their orthologs in the Y. lipolytica genome.
source: We did not find any density at positions of the mammalian 42 kDa subunit (NDUFA10), the 9 kDa subunit (NDUFV3), or the MNLL (NDUFB1) subunit, consistent with the absence of their orthologs in the Y. lipolytica genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and genomic data.

claim: The absence of the MNLL subunit correlates with a shift of the adjacent TMH1 in ND4.
source: The absence of the MNLL subunit correlates with a shift of the adjacent TMH1 in ND4 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 7.

claim: Subunit NUXM was modelled next to the first three helices of central subunit ND2, which are absent in mammalian complex I.
source: We modelled subunit NUXM that has no correspondence in vertebrates next to the first three helices of central subunit ND2, which are absent in mammalian complex I (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the model building process.

claim: The assignment of NUXM is based on the allocation of NUXM to the PP module, secondary structure prediction, and a short stretch of sequence with side chains.
source: This assignment is based on the allocation of NUXM to the PP module (Angerer et al., 2011), secondary structure prediction, and a short stretch of sequence with side chains.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the assignment.

claim: Subunit N7BM shares an extensive interface with ST1.
source: We now show that N7BM shares an extensive interface with ST1, and that ST1 furthermore interacts with NUZM and the N-terminal region of the 30 kDa subunit (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: ST1 interacts with NUZM and the N-terminal region of the 30 kDa subunit.
source: We now show that N7BM shares an extensive interface with ST1, and that ST1 furthermore interacts with NUZM and the N-terminal region of the 30 kDa subunit (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Four lipid molecules were identified in the membrane arm.
source: Four lipid molecules were identified in the membrane arm.
evidence: This is a direct statement of structural findings.

claim: A prominent density in the interior of subunit ND1 towards the interface with the PSST and 49 kDa subunits was not assigned unambiguously.
source: A prominent density in the interior of subunit ND1 towards the interface with the PSST and 49 kDa subunits was not assigned unambiguously (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a statement about an unassigned density in the structure.

claim: The most prominent part of the unassigned density was in direct contact with side chains of conserved Arg36ND1, Arg297ND1 and Leu20049-kDa, and close to the conserved Arg27ND1 and Arg108PSST.
source: The most prominent part of this density was in direct contact with side chains of conserved Arg36ND1, Arg297ND1 and Leu20049-kDa, and close to the conserved Arg27ND1 and Arg108PSST.
evidence: This is a structural observation about the unassigned density.

claim: The unassigned density is close to or even within the proposed access pathway by which ubiquinone enters the active site.
source: The density is remarkable because it is close to or even within the proposed access pathway by which ubiquinone enters the active site.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Recent MD simulations suggested that the residues corresponding to Arg27ND1 and Arg108PSST in bovine complex I would coordinate part of the isoprenoid side chain of ubiquinone by π-stacking of their guanidinium groups.
source: Recent MD simulations suggested that the residues corresponding to Arg27ND1 and Arg108PSST in bovine complex I would coordinate part of the isoprenoid side chain of ubiquinone by π-stacking of their guanidinium groups (Fedor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The narrow and well-defined contact sites with Arg36ND1 and Arg297ND1 are consistent with a strong ionic interaction.
source: In contrast, the narrow and well-defined contact sites with Arg36ND1 and Arg297ND1 we observe are consistent with a strong ionic interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The unassigned density appears to be too bulky for an isoprenoid chain or even for a ubiquinone head group.
source: The density appears to be too bulky for an isoprenoid chain or even for a ubiquinone head group.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density.

claim: The density represents the negatively charged head group of a lipid molecule.
source: We therefore suggest that the density represents the negatively charged head group of a lipid molecule.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural data.

claim: More than 60 lipid molecules per complex I were bound in the preparation as detected by mass spectrometry.
source: More than 60 lipid molecules per complex I were bound in our preparation as detected by mass spectrometry (Table 3), but at our current map resolution their densities cannot be assigned unequivocally.
evidence: This is a direct statement of mass spectrometry results.

claim: At the current map resolution, lipid densities cannot be assigned unequivocally.
source: More than 60 lipid molecules per complex I were bound in our preparation as detected by mass spectrometry (Table 3), but at our current map resolution their densities cannot be assigned unequivocally.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current resolution.

claim: A lipid head group would be consistent with the complementary charges of conserved arginine residues in this area.
source: A lipid head group would be consistent with the complementary charges of conserved arginine residues in this area, although it would be situated at an unusual position above the membrane surface.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The same density was found under turnover conditions.
source: The same density was found under turnover conditions (see below) and therefore obviously did not prevent the passage of ubiquinone to its binding site.
evidence: This is a comparison between the deactive and turnover structures.

claim: The density did not prevent the passage of ubiquinone to its binding site.
source: The same density was found under turnover conditions (see below) and therefore obviously did not prevent the passage of ubiquinone to its binding site.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the density is present during turnover.

claim: A lipid molecule in this position might partly block the generally accepted ubiquinone access pathway through the portal formed by TMH1, TMH6, and helix α1–2 of ND1.
source: Although a lipid molecule in this position might partly block the generally accepted ubiquinone access pathway through the portal formed by TMH1, TMH6, and helix α1–2 of ND1, it would be flexible and mobile enough to allow ubiquinone access, while keeping other hydrophilic compounds out, acting like a hydrophobic valve.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the function of the lipid.

claim: The lipid would be flexible and mobile enough to allow ubiquinone access, while keeping other hydrophilic compounds out, acting like a hydrophobic valve.
source: Although a lipid molecule in this position might partly block the generally accepted ubiquinone access pathway through the portal formed by TMH1, TMH6, and helix α1–2 of ND1, it would be flexible and mobile enough to allow ubiquinone access, while keeping other hydrophilic compounds out, acting like a hydrophobic valve.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the function of the lipid.

claim: The ubiquinone binding and access site is essentially formed by the hydrophilic PSST and 49 kDa subunits and the membrane-intrinsic ND1 subunit.
source: The ubiquinone binding and access site is essentially formed by the hydrophilic PSST and 49 kDa subunits and the membrane-intrinsic ND1 subunit (Zickermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In recent cryo-EM structures of deactive mammalian complex I, critical loops of the 49 kDa, ND1, ND3 and 39 kDa subunits were proposed to unfold, because no matching density was found.
source: In recent cryo-EM structures of deactive mammalian complex I, critical loops of the latter two subunits and of the adjacent ND3 and the accessory 39 kDa subunits were proposed to unfold, because no matching density was found (Blaza et al., 2018; Agip et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In the Y. lipolytica map only residues 35 – 48 in the central part of the long TMH1-2 loop of subunit ND3 were disordered.
source: In our map only residues 35 – 48 in the central part of the long TMH1-2 loop of subunit ND3 were disordered (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 10.

claim: In contrast to bovine complex I, continuous density was observed for the loop connecting the first two β-strands of the 49 kDa subunit.
source: In contrast to bovine complex I, we observed continuous density for the loop connecting the first two β-strands of the 49 kDa subunit and for the TMH5-6 loop of ND1.
evidence: This is a comparison with bovine complex I.

claim: In contrast to bovine complex I, continuous density was observed for the TMH5-6 loop of ND1.
source: In contrast to bovine complex I, we observed continuous density for the loop connecting the first two β-strands of the 49 kDa subunit and for the TMH5-6 loop of ND1.
evidence: This is a comparison with bovine complex I.

claim: The local resolution of the ubiquinone binding region indicated some degree of flexibility, and it was therefore modelled as poly-alanine.
source: The local resolution of this region indicated some degree of flexibility, and it was therefore modelled as poly-alanine.
evidence: This is a statement about the modelling approach based on map quality.

claim: The C-terminal domain of accessory subunit NUEM was largely modelled with side chains.
source: The C-terminal domain of accessory subunit NUEM, which is supposed to have a regulatory function in the A/D transition (Babot et al., 2014), was largely modelled with side chains, whereas the corresponding domain in the mammalian 39 kDa subunit was disordered.
evidence: This is a statement about the model and a comparison with mammalian complex I.

claim: The C-terminal domain of NUEM is supposed to have a regulatory function in the A/D transition.
source: The C-terminal domain of accessory subunit NUEM, which is supposed to have a regulatory function in the A/D transition (Babot et al., 2014), was largely modelled with side chains, whereas the corresponding domain in the mammalian 39 kDa subunit was disordered.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The corresponding domain in the mammalian 39 kDa subunit was disordered.
source: The C-terminal domain of accessory subunit NUEM, which is supposed to have a regulatory function in the A/D transition (Babot et al., 2014), was largely modelled with side chains, whereas the corresponding domain in the mammalian 39 kDa subunit was disordered.
evidence: This is a comparison with mammalian complex I.

claim: Ubiquinone is hydrophobic and even the short-chain analogue decylubiquinone (DBQ) is not soluble in aqueous buffers at sufficiently high concentrations.
source: Ubiquinone is hydrophobic and even the short-chain analogue decylubiquinone (DBQ) used in this study is not soluble in aqueous buffers at sufficiently high concentrations.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical properties of ubiquinone.

claim: To avoid substrate exhaustion, the temperature of the reaction was reduced to 18°C and 1 µM ubiquinol oxidase from Vitreoscilla sp. was added to recycle the ubiquinone.
source: To avoid substrate exhaustion at 2 µM complex I concentration between adding the substrate and freezing the sample, we reduced the temperature of the reaction to 18°C and added 1 µM ubiquinol oxidase from Vitreoscilla sp. to recycle the ubiquinone.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: An increase in oxidase concentration did not increase the rate of oxygen consumption, indicating that complex I was rate-limiting and that ubiquinone oxidation was efficient.
source: An increase in oxidase concentration did not increase the rate of oxygen consumption, indicating that complex I was rate-limiting and that ubiquinone oxidation was efficient.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental observations.

claim: Recycling of substrate by this artificial respiratory chain sustained steady-state conditions for more than one minute.
source: Recycling of substrate by this artificial respiratory chain sustained steady-state conditions for more than one minute, while freezing the cryo-EM sample took only 20–30 s (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions shown in Figure 11.

claim: Freezing the cryo-EM sample took only 20–30 s.
source: Recycling of substrate by this artificial respiratory chain sustained steady-state conditions for more than one minute, while freezing the cryo-EM sample took only 20–30 s (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The structure of complex I under turnover conditions indicated no overall changes compared to the deactive state.
source: The structure of complex I under turnover conditions indicated no overall changes compared to the deactive state.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two structures.

claim: Large conformational rearrangements, such as the proposed extensive movement of the two arms relative to one another, can be excluded.
source: We can therefore exclude large conformational rearrangements, such as the proposed extensive movement of the two arms relative to one another (Böttcher et al., 2002) (Figure 12).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural comparison shown in Figure 12.

claim: No evidence was found for a piston-like movement of the long lateral helix of the membrane arm that has been proposed to couple redox chemistry to proton translocation.
source: We also found no evidence for a piston-like movement of the long lateral helix of the membrane arm that has been proposed to couple redox chemistry to proton translocation (Hunte et al., 2010; Baradaran et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of a proposed conformational change, citing previous literature.

claim: The most obvious difference between deactive and turnover states was a strong additional density in the 51 kDa subunit, which was modelled as bound NADH.
source: The most obvious difference was a strong additional density in the 51 kDa subunit, which was modelled as bound NADH (Figure 13A) in agreement with a previous structure of bacterial complex I (Berrisford and Sazanov, 2009).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 13A and compared with previous work.

claim: A slight movement of the glycine-rich loop (Gly88-Gly91) opens the site to accommodate the substrate in this position.
source: A slight movement of the glycine-rich loop (Gly88-Gly91) opens the site to accommodate the substrate in this position.
evidence: This is a structural observation about conformational changes upon NADH binding.

claim: The pyridine ring moiety engages in a tight stacking interaction with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN to allow efficient hydride transfer.
source: The pyridine ring moiety engages in a tight stacking interaction with the isoalloxazine ring of FMN to allow efficient hydride transfer.
evidence: This is a structural observation about the NADH binding mode.

claim: The adenine ring interacts by π-stacking with Phe92, Phe100, and Phe231 of the 51 kDa subunit.
source: The adenine ring interacts by π-stacking with Phe92, Phe100, and Phe231 of the 51 kDa subunit.
evidence: This is a structural observation about NADH binding interactions.

claim: Lys228 forms a salt bridge with the pyrophosphate of NADH.
source: Lys228 forms a salt bridge with the pyrophosphate, and Ser325 establishes a hydrogen bond to a ribose group of the bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is a structural observation about NADH binding interactions.

claim: Ser325 establishes a hydrogen bond to a ribose group of the bound nucleotide.
source: Lys228 forms a salt bridge with the pyrophosphate, and Ser325 establishes a hydrogen bond to a ribose group of the bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is a structural observation about NADH binding interactions.

claim: In the 49 kDa subunit a change in the structure of the β1-β2 loop of the N-terminal β sheet was observed, which widens the central cavity formed by this subunit and subunit PSST.
source: In the 49 kDa subunit we observed a change in the structure of the β1-β2 loop of the N-terminal β sheet, which widens the central cavity formed by this subunit and subunit PSST.
evidence: This is a structural observation comparing deactive and turnover states.

claim: A clear density consistent with a ubiquinone head group was found between the 49 kDa subunit β1-β2 loop and the α2 helix of subunit PSST.
source: A clear density consistent with a ubiquinone head group was found between the 49 kDa subunit β1-β2 loop and the α2 helix of subunit PSST (Figure 13B,C).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 13B,C.

claim: The position of the ubiquinone head group closely matches that of a ubiquinone-antagonistic inhibitor in the X-ray structure of Y. lipolytica complex I, as identified by anomalous scattering of bromine-substituted inhibitor.
source: This position closely matches that of a ubiquinone-antagonistic inhibitor in the X-ray structure of Y. lipolytica complex I, as identified by anomalous scattering of bromine-substituted inhibitor (Figure 13D) (Zickermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous structural work shown in Figure 13D.

claim: The new density represents the headgroup of a bound ubiquinone substrate at a minimal edge-to-edge distance of ~12 Å from cluster N2.
source: We conclude that the new density represents the headgroup of a bound ubiquinone substrate at a minimal edge-to-edge distance of ~12 Å from cluster N2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: This ubiquinone binding site is different from the ubiquinone binding site reported for the bacterial enzyme from T. thermophilus.
source: This site is different from the ubiquinone binding site reported for the bacterial enzyme from T. thermophilus, which engages a strictly conserved tyrosine adjacent to the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 and positions the quinone headgroup ~2 Å closer to cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013) (Figure 14A).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous structural work shown in Figure 14A.

claim: The bacterial ubiquinone binding site engages a strictly conserved tyrosine adjacent to the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 and positions the quinone headgroup ~2 Å closer to cluster N2.
source: This site is different from the ubiquinone binding site reported for the bacterial enzyme from T. thermophilus, which engages a strictly conserved tyrosine adjacent to the terminal iron-sulfur cluster N2 and positions the quinone headgroup ~2 Å closer to cluster N2 (Baradaran et al., 2013) (Figure 14A).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and shown in Figure 14A.

claim: There is abundant evidence from site-directed mutagenesis in Y. lipolytica to support substrate and inhibitor binding to the conserved tyrosine.
source: There is abundant evidence from site-directed mutagenesis in Y. lipolytica to support substrate and inhibitor binding to this tyrosine (Tocilescu et al., 2010), suggesting that this binding site also exists in the mitochondrial enzyme and that it alternates with the site observed in the structure of complex I under turnover conditions, as presented here.
evidence: This is cited from previous mutagenesis studies.

claim: The tyrosine binding site also exists in the mitochondrial enzyme and alternates with the site observed in the structure of complex I under turnover conditions.
source: There is abundant evidence from site-directed mutagenesis in Y. lipolytica to support substrate and inhibitor binding to this tyrosine (Tocilescu et al., 2010), suggesting that this binding site also exists in the mitochondrial enzyme and that it alternates with the site observed in the structure of complex I under turnover conditions, as presented here.
evidence: This is an inference based on mutagenesis data and the current structural findings.

claim: Two different models for the structural basis of the A/D transition of complex I have recently been proposed.
source: Two different models for the structural basis of the A/D transition of complex I have recently been proposed.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: In the X-ray structure of the deactive form of Y. lipolytica complex I, access of a ubiquinone-antagonistic inhibitor into a binding position close to cluster N2 was blocked by a specific conformation of the β1-β2 loop of the 49 kDa subunit.
source: In the X-ray structure of the deactive form of Y. lipolytica complex I (Zickermann et al., 2015), access of a ubiquinone-antagonistic inhibitor into a binding position close to cluster N2 was blocked by a specific conformation of the β1-β2 loop of the 49 kDa subunit.
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: The authors hypothesized that during the A/D transition the interface region of complex I can switch between two defined conformational states and that the A- and D-forms of complex I are tightly linked with intermediates of the catalytic cycle.
source: We hypothesized that during the A/D transition the interface region of complex I can switch between two defined conformational states and that the A- and D-forms of complex I are tightly linked with intermediates of the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The 'unfolded Q site model' for the A/D transition describes the D-form as an 'off pathway' intermediate that is characterized by extensive relaxation of several loops in and around the ubiquinone binding cavity.
source: In contrast, the 'unfolded Q site model' for the A/D transition (Blaza et al., 2018) describes the D-form as an 'off pathway' intermediate that is characterized by extensive relaxation of several loops in and around the ubiquinone binding cavity.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: According to the 'unfolded Q site model', ubiquinone is required to restructure the interface region during transition into the A-form.
source: According to this model, ubiquinone is required to restructure the interface region during transition into the A-form.
evidence: This is a description of the 'unfolded Q site model'.

claim: Blaza et al. speculated that a corresponding loss of defined protein structure in the deactive Y. lipolytica complex I was prevented by a bound inhibitor molecule.
source: Blaza et al. speculated that a corresponding loss of defined protein structure in the deactive Y. lipolytica complex I was prevented by a bound inhibitor molecule.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The speculation that a bound inhibitor prevented unfolding in Y. lipolytica can now be excluded, as in the current cryo-EM structure no inhibitor was present.
source: However, this can now be excluded, as in our cryo-EM structure of Y. lipolytica complex I no inhibitor was present.
evidence: This is an inference from the current structural data.

claim: Unfolding of the ubiquinone reduction site was not observed in Y. lipolytica, at least not to an extent comparable to mammalian complex I.
source: Yet unfolding of the ubiquinone reduction site was not observed, at least not to an extent comparable to mammalian complex I.
evidence: This is a comparison of the Y. lipolytica structure with mammalian structures.

claim: The species-dependent degrees of disorder in this critical region of complex I may reflect the significantly higher energy barrier for the A/D transition in bovine complex I as compared to Y. lipolytica.
source: The species-dependent degrees of disorder in this critical region of complex I may reflect the significantly higher energy barrier for the A/D transition in bovine complex I as compared to Y. lipolytica (Maklashina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison of structures and cited kinetic data.

claim: In mouse complex I the interface between accessory subunits NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 changes during the A/D transition; strong contacts between the two subunits seem to selectively stabilize the A form.
source: It is interesting to note that in mouse complex I the interface between accessory subunits NDUFA5 and NDUFA10 changes during the A/D transition; strong contacts between the two subunits seem to selectively stabilize the A form (Agip et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: This effect can be excluded for the Y. lipolytica complex, because it does not have an NDUFA10 ortholog.
source: This effect can be excluded for the Y. lipolytica complex, because it does not have an NDUFA10 ortholog.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of NDUFA10 in Y. lipolytica.

claim: Ubiquinone reduction releases the energy for proton translocation.
source: Ubiquinone reduction releases the energy for proton translocation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about complex I mechanism.

claim: The ubiquinone reduction site has to play a central role in energy conversion.
source: The ubiquinone reduction site therefore has to play a central role in energy conversion.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the role of ubiquinone reduction.

claim: The data provide direct evidence for the earlier proposal of a second binding site for ubiquinone within the substrate binding pocket of complex I.
source: Our data provide direct evidence for our earlier proposal of a second binding site for ubiquinone within the substrate binding pocket of complex I (Zickermann et al., 2015), which becomes dominant during steady-state turnover.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the current findings in relation to previous work.

claim: The second ubiquinone binding site becomes dominant during steady-state turnover.
source: Our data provide direct evidence for our earlier proposal of a second binding site for ubiquinone within the substrate binding pocket of complex I (Zickermann et al., 2015), which becomes dominant during steady-state turnover.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: As compared to the D-form, under turnover conditions the only notable difference observed nearby was a reorganization of the β1-β2-loop of the 49 kDa subunit.
source: As compared to the D-form, under turnover conditions the only notable difference observed nearby was a reorganization of the β1-β2-loop of the 49 kDa subunit (Figure 13B,C).
evidence: This is a comparison of the two structures shown in Figure 13B,C.

claim: The critical loop connecting TMH1 and TMH2 of ND3 is flexible in both states.
source: The critical loop connecting TMH1 and TMH2 of ND3 is flexible in both states (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 10.

claim: These findings support the proposed integrated functional model, which suggests that the structural changes associated with the A/D transition and the catalytic cycle of complex I are in fact closely linked.
source: These findings support our proposed integrated functional model, which suggests that the structural changes associated with the A/D transition and the catalytic cycle of complex I are in fact closely linked (Zickermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to the proposed model.

claim: According to the integrated functional model, the D-form represents the enzyme locked in an intermediate state of the catalytic cycle termed P-state in the proposed two-state stabilization-change mechanism.
source: According to this model, the D-form represents the enzyme locked in an intermediate state of the catalytic cycle termed P-state in the proposed two-state stabilization-change mechanism (Brandt, 2011) (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the proposed model shown in Figure 14B.

claim: The E-state would be characterized by a ubiquinone binding site closer to iron-sulfur cluster N2.
source: The E-state would be characterized by a ubiquinone binding site closer to iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Figure 14A), which so far was observed only in the oxidized bacterial enzyme (Baradaran et al., 2013) that does not undergo the A/D transition.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison with bacterial structures shown in Figure 14A.

claim: The E-state was so far observed only in the oxidized bacterial enzyme that does not undergo the A/D transition.
source: The E-state would be characterized by a ubiquinone binding site closer to iron-sulfur cluster N2 (Figure 14A), which so far was observed only in the oxidized bacterial enzyme (Baradaran et al., 2013) that does not undergo the A/D transition.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: A larger distance between the ubiquinone headgroup and its primary electron donor is in principle consistent with the impaired reduction in the P-state, as predicted by the mechanistic model.
source: A larger distance between the ubiquinone headgroup and its primary electron donor is in principle consistent with the impaired reduction in the P-state, as predicted by the mechanistic model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data in relation to the mechanistic model.

claim: The observed 12 Å distance between the ubiquinone headgroup and cluster N2 in the P-state is within the <14 Å range that would still allow efficient electron transfer according to the 'Moser-Dutton ruler'.
source: The observed 12 Å distance between the ubiquinone headgroup and cluster N2 in the P-state is within the <14 Å range that would still allow efficient electron transfer according to the 'Moser-Dutton ruler' (Moser et al., 2010) commonly used to estimate electron tunnelling rates between redox centres in proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the distance measurement in relation to electron transfer theory.

claim: In the present case, electron transfer is linked to protonation, and therefore other parameters, such as reorganization energy and packing density, have to be taken into consideration.
source: However, in the present case, electron transfer is linked to protonation, and therefore other parameters, such as reorganization energy and packing density, have to be taken into consideration.
evidence: This is a statement about the complexity of the electron transfer process.

claim: These parameters are likely to slow down electron transfer sufficiently for the mechanistic model proposed, even at the short distance observed for the P-state.
source: These parameters do not depend simply on distance but on the local protein environment. They are likely to slow down electron transfer sufficiently for the mechanistic model we propose, even at the short distance observed for the P-state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the electron transfer kinetics.

claim: In the catalytic cycle, the E-state is predicted to be short-lived under the uncoupled steady-state turnover conditions applied, explaining the observed predominance of the P-state.
source: In the catalytic cycle, the E-state is predicted to be short-lived under the uncoupled steady-state turnover conditions applied here, explaining the observed predominance of the P-state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the structural observations.

claim: Once bound to the E-site, ubiquinone is rapidly reduced by iron sulfur-cluster N2, which essentially remains reduced on the time scale of catalytic turnover.
source: Once bound to the E-site, ubiquinone is rapidly reduced by iron sulfur-cluster N2, which essentially remains reduced on the time scale of catalytic turnover (Krishnamoorthy and Hinkle, 1988) (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and illustrated in Figure 14B.

claim: The resulting highly unstable semiquinone then rapidly triggers the E → P conversion, creating the alternate binding site for the ubiquinone headgroup.
source: The resulting highly unstable semiquinone then rapidly triggers the E → P conversion, creating the alternate binding site for the ubiquinone headgroup (Zickermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism cited from previous work.

claim: These rearrangements are driven by thermodynamic stabilization of the charged ubiquinone intermediate that provides the energy for the electrostatic power stroke.
source: These rearrangements are driven by thermodynamic stabilization of the charged ubiquinone intermediate that provides the energy for the electrostatic power stroke (Brandt, 2011).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism cited from previous work.

claim: The power stroke is transmitted through the chain of protonable residues into the membrane arm, where it ultimately drives proton pumping.
source: The power stroke is then transmitted through the chain of protonable residues into the membrane arm, where it ultimately drives proton pumping (Figure 14C).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 14C.

claim: Subsequently, neutral semiquinone produced by protonation in the P-state allows the system to return to the E-state.
source: Subsequently, neutral semiquinone produced by protonation in the P-state allows the system to return to the E-state.
evidence: This is part of the proposed catalytic cycle.

claim: The semiquinone then picks up the second electron to trigger another power stroke driven by the stabilization of the ubiquinol anion.
source: The semiquinone then picks up the second electron to trigger another power stroke driven by the stabilization of the ubiquinol anion (Figure 14B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed catalytic cycle illustrated in Figure 14B.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of mitochondrial complex I under turnover conditions corroborates several predictions of the proposed two-state stabilization change mechanism.
source: In summary, our cryo-EM structure of mitochondrial complex I under turnover conditions corroborates several predictions of the proposed two-state stabilization change mechanism and how it relates to the regulatory A/D transition.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: The new structure provides strong support for the integrated functional model that describes the structural basis of energy conversion and regulation in respiratory complex I.
source: Our new structure provides strong support for our integrated functional model that describes the structural basis of energy conversion and regulation in respiratory complex I.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Under standard assay conditions (60 µM DBQ, no added lipid or detergent) the preparation had an activity of 1.8 µMol−1mg−1min−1.
source: Under our standard assay conditions (60 µM DBQ, no added lipid or detergent) the preparation had an activity of 1.8 µMol−1mg−1min−1, increasing to 5.9 µMol−1mg−1min−1 upon lipid reactivation (Dröse et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental measurements.

claim: The activity increased to 5.9 µMol−1mg−1min−1 upon lipid reactivation.
source: Under our standard assay conditions (60 µM DBQ, no added lipid or detergent) the preparation had an activity of 1.8 µMol−1mg−1min−1, increasing to 5.9 µMol−1mg−1min−1 upon lipid reactivation (Dröse et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental measurements.

claim: Using the assay conditions established for bovine complex I (200 µM DBQ, 0.15% asolectin, 0.15% CHAPS) the activity of the preparation was 13.9 µMol−1mg−1min−1.
source: Using the assay conditions established for bovine complex I (200 µM DBQ, 0.15% asolectin, 0.15% CHAPS) (Blaza et al., 2018) the activity of the preparation was 13.9 µMol−1mg−1min−1.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental measurements.
